HOME INSPECTOR STANDARDS OF PRACTICE AND LIABILITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's home inspector standards of practice, conflict-of-interest, and liability rules (Business and Professions Code §§ 7195-7199) as they may apply to a home inspection of the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, ordered by Jordan Lee and, if named, performed by Bay Area Home Inspections, Inc. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not authorize, direct, or perform any home inspection, and it does not resolve whether any particular inspector, inspection, report, or repair complies with these statutes.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "HOME INSPECTION," "MATERIAL DEFECT," AND "HOME INSPECTOR"
California's Business and Professions Code defines several terms used throughout its home inspector chapter (Chapter 9.3, §§ 7195-7199). A "home inspection" is a noninvasive, physical examination, performed for a fee in connection with a transfer of real property, of the mechanical, electrical, or plumbing systems or the structural and essential components of a residential dwelling of one to four units, designed to identify material defects in those systems, structures, and components; the term also includes any consultation regarding the property that is represented to be a home inspection or any confusingly similar term. A "material defect" is a condition that significantly affects the value, desirability, habitability, or safety of the dwelling, and the statute specifies that style or aesthetics are not to be considered in determining whether a system, structure, or component is defective. A "home inspector" is any individual who performs a home inspection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "“Home inspection” is a noninvasive, physical examination, performed for a fee in connection with a transfer, as defined in subdivision (e), of real property, of the mechanical, electrical, or plumbing systems or the structural and essential components of a residential dwelling of one to four units designed to identify material defects in those systems, structures, and components. “Home inspection” includes any consultation regarding the property that is represented to be a home inspection or any confusingly similar term."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7195(a)(1), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "home inspection" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7195.)
  "“material defect” is a condition that significantly affects the value, desirability, habitability, or safety of the dwelling. Style or aesthetics shall not be considered in determining whether a system, structure, or component is defective."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7195(b), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "material defect" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7195.)
  "“home inspector” is any individual who performs a home inspection."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7195(d), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "home inspector" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7195.)
  Known gap: This clause states the chapter's core definitions only. The statute also defines additional terms not quoted here, including a pool/spa-specific component of the "home inspection" definition tied to Health and Safety Code § 115922's drowning-prevention safety features, and an optional energy-efficiency inspection component -- this document does not restate those subparts. It also does not determine, for any specific individual or engagement, whether a given examination in fact meets this definition of "home inspection" or whether a given condition is a "material defect."

"HOME INSPECTION REPORT" CONTENT AND THE TRANSACTIONS THE CHAPTER COVERS
The statute also defines the written product of a home inspection and the kinds of real estate transactions its chapter addresses. A "home inspection report" is a written report prepared for a fee and issued after a home inspection; the report clearly describes and identifies the inspected systems, structures, or components of the dwelling, any material defects identified, and any recommendations regarding the conditions observed or recommendations for evaluation by appropriate persons. "Transfer" is defined broadly for purposes of the chapter: a transfer by sale, exchange, installment land sales contract, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, of real property or a residential stock cooperative, improved with or consisting of not less than one nor more than four dwelling units.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A “home inspection report” is a written report prepared for a fee and issued after a home inspection. The report clearly describes and identifies the inspected systems, structures, or components of the dwelling, any material defects identified, and any recommendations regarding the conditions observed or recommendations for evaluation by appropriate persons."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7195(c), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "home inspection report" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7195.)
  "“Transfer” is a transfer by sale, exchange, installment land sales contract, as defined in Section 2985 of the Civil Code, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, of real property or residential stock cooperative, improved with or consisting of not less than one nor more than four dwelling units."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7195(e), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "transfer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7195.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general "home inspection report" definition and the general "transfer" definition only. Section 7195(c) also contains pool/spa-specific reporting content (tied to Health and Safety Code §§ 115922-115923) not restated here. This document does not determine, for any specific document or transaction, whether it meets these definitions.

STATUTORY STANDARD OF CARE
California's Business and Professions Code fixes a standard of care for a defined category of home inspectors. It is the duty of a home inspector who is not licensed as a general contractor, structural pest control operator, or architect, or registered as a professional engineer, to conduct a home inspection with the degree of care that a reasonably prudent home inspector would exercise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "It is the duty of a home inspector who is not licensed as a general contractor, structural pest control operator, or architect, or registered as a professional engineer to conduct a home inspection with the degree of care that a reasonably prudent home inspector would exercise."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7196, California Business and Professions Code, home inspector standard of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7196.)
  Known gap: By its own terms, this specific statutory duty of care is stated for a home inspector who is not licensed as a general contractor, structural pest control operator, or architect, or registered as a professional engineer. This document does not determine what standard of care applies to a home inspection performed by someone who does hold one of those licenses or registrations, or whether any given inspection met the "reasonably prudent home inspector" standard.

CONFLICT-OF-INTEREST AND REFERRAL PRACTICES DEFINED AS UNFAIR
California's Business and Professions Code identifies specific practices by a home inspector, an employing company, or a company controlled by a company with a financial interest in an employing company, as an unfair business practice. It is an unfair business practice for a home inspector, a company that employs the inspector, or a company that is controlled by a company that also has a financial interest in a company employing a home inspector, to do any of the following: to perform or offer to perform, for an additional fee, any repairs to a structure on which the inspector or the inspector's company has prepared a home inspection report in the past 12 months; to inspect for a fee any property in which the inspector or the inspector's company has any financial interest or any interest in the transfer of the property; to offer or deliver any compensation, inducement, or reward to the owner of the inspected property, the broker, or agent, for the referral of any business to the inspector or the inspection company; or to accept an engagement to make an inspection or prepare a report in which the employment itself or the fee payable for the inspection is contingent upon the conclusions in the report, preestablished findings, or the close of escrow. A home protection company that is affiliated with or that retains the home inspector does not violate this section if it performs repairs pursuant to claims made under the home protection contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "It is an unfair business practice for a home inspector, a company that employs the inspector, or a company that is controlled by a company that also has a financial interest in a company employing a home inspector, to do any of the following: (1) To perform or offer to perform, for an additional fee, any repairs to a structure on which the inspector, or the inspector’s company, has prepared a home inspection report in the past 12 months. (2) Inspect for a fee any property in which the inspector, or the inspector’s company, has any financial interest or any interest in the transfer of the property. (3) To offer or deliver any compensation, inducement, or reward to the owner of the inspected property, the broker, or agent, for the referral of any business to the inspector or the inspection company. (4) Accept an engagement to make an inspection or to prepare a report in which the employment itself or the fee payable for the inspection is contingent upon the conclusions in the report, preestablished findings, or the close of escrow."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7197(a), California Business and Professions Code, home inspector unfair business practices (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7197.)
  "A home protection company that is affiliated with or that retains the home inspector does not violate this section if it performs repairs pursuant to claims made under the home protection contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7197(b), California Business and Professions Code, home protection company exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7197.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general prohibitions of § 7197(a) and the home-protection-company exception in § 7197(b). It does not state § 7197(c) (concerning structural pest control operator repairs under Business and Professions Code § 8505) or the roofing- and plumbing-contractor exceptions in § 7197(d)-(e), which are addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether any specific arrangement falls within one of these prohibitions or exceptions.

ROOFING AND PLUMBING CONTRACTOR EXCEPTIONS TO THE REPAIR PROHIBITION
The statute carves out two specific, conditioned exceptions to the paragraph (a)(1) prohibition on a home inspector performing repairs on a structure the inspector's company recently inspected. Paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) shall not affect the ability of a roofing contractor who holds a C-39 license, as defined in Section 832.39 of Title 16 of the California Code of Regulations, to perform repairs pursuant to the contractor's inspection of a roof for the specific purpose of providing a roof certification if all of the following conditions are met, including that different employees perform the home inspection and the roof inspection, that the roof inspection is ordered before or at the same time as the home inspection or completed before the home inspection begins, and that the consumer receives a specified disclosure before authorizing the home inspection. Paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) shall not affect the ability of a plumbing contractor who holds a C-36 license, as defined in Section 832.36 of Title 16 of the California Code of Regulations, to perform repairs pursuant to the inspection of a sewer lateral pipe connecting a residence or business to a sewer system if the consumer is provided a consumer disclosure before the consumer authorizes the home inspection that includes all of the following notifications, including that the same company performing the sewer lateral inspection and repairs will perform the home inspection, that authorized repairs are limited to those identified in the sewer lateral inspection report, and that the consumer has the right to seek a second opinion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) shall not affect the ability of a roofing contractor who holds a C-39 license, as defined in Section 832.39 of Title 16 of the California Code of Regulations, to perform repairs pursuant to the contractor’s inspection of a roof for the specific purpose of providing a roof certification if all of the following conditions are met:"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7197(d), California Business and Professions Code, roofing contractor (C-39) exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7197.)
  "Paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) shall not affect the ability of a plumbing contractor who holds a C-36 license, as defined in Section 832.36 of Title 16 of the California Code of Regulations, to perform repairs pursuant to the inspection of a sewer lateral pipe connecting a residence or business to a sewer system if the consumer is provided a consumer disclosure before the consumer authorizes the home inspection that includes all of the following notifications:"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7197(e), California Business and Professions Code, plumbing contractor (C-36) sewer lateral exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7197.)
  Known gap: This clause states the introductory conditions of the § 7197(d) roofing exception and the § 7197(e) plumbing exception in summary form; the numbered sub-conditions of each exception (the specific content each consumer disclosure must include) are described in this clause's body in summarized, non-quoted form rather than quoted verbatim. This document does not determine whether any specific roofing or plumbing contractor's disclosure or repair satisfies these conditions.

CONTRACTUAL WAIVERS OF THE DUTY OF CARE ARE INVALID
California's Business and Professions Code addresses attempts to contract around the § 7196 duty of care or to cap liability. Contractual provisions that purport to waive the duty owed pursuant to Section 7196, or limit the liability of the home inspector to the cost of the home inspection report, are contrary to public policy and invalid.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Contractual provisions that purport to waive the duty owed pursuant to Section 7196, or limit the liability of the home inspector to the cost of the home inspection report, are contrary to public policy and invalid."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7198, California Business and Professions Code, invalidity of duty-waiver and liability-limitation clauses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7198.)
  Known gap: This document does not determine whether any specific contract clause is, in fact, a provision that purports to waive the § 7196 duty or limit liability to the cost of the report, nor does it address remedies available once such a provision is found invalid.

FOUR-YEAR STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS FOR HOME INSPECTION REPORT CLAIMS
California's Business and Professions Code sets a specific limitations period for legal actions arising from a home inspection report. The time for commencement of a legal action for breach of duty arising from a home inspection report shall not exceed four years from the date of the inspection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The time for commencement of a legal action for breach of duty arising from a home inspection report shall not exceed four years from the date of the inspection."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7199, California Business and Professions Code, four-year statute of limitations for home inspection report claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7199.)
  Known gap: This document does not determine the date of inspection for any specific engagement, whether any tolling doctrine might apply, or how this four-year period interacts with limitations periods that might separately apply to other claims (for example, claims against a seller for nondisclosure) arising from the same transaction.

It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific inspection, report, or repair question.
